title: Children's rights: UNCRC, Human Rights Act 1998 and the voice of the child
blurb: Link everyday children's nursing to UNCRC articles and Human Rights Act rights, and put the child's own voice at the centre of care.
question: A children's ward plans to close its playroom to make space for an extra bed bay. The play specialist objects that this breaches the children's rights. Which right is she most likely relying on, and how strong is it in English law?

teach.body: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC, adopted 1989) is an international treaty the UK has ratified: it shapes policy and professional standards but is not directly enforceable in English courts. The Human Rights Act 1998 brings the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law: NHS bodies are public authorities and must act compatibly with Convention rights, and people can bring claims in UK courts. In plain English: the UNCRC sets the standard; the HRA is the enforceable law.

teach.caption: Wales and Scotland have their own measures giving the UNCRC more legal force.

teach.body: UNCRC Article 12 gives children the right to express their views on matters affecting them, given due weight according to age and maturity. The same idea runs through English law: the first item on the Children Act s1(3) welfare checklist is the child's wishes and feelings, and Working Together 2026 asks practitioners to keep the child in focus. In practice: speak to the child, not just the parent; use their words in records; offer real choices.

steps.label: Listen
steps.sub: Without the parent answering for them

teach.caption: NICE NG213 1.4.13: record the child's own words in their preferred format, without rewriting them.

teach.h: Applying it: Ayo, 8, and the cannula
teach.body: Ayo needs a cannula. The nurse asks which hand he draws with, explains the options with a play specialist, and lets him choose the site and whether to watch. Treatment is not optional, but how it happens can be. This respects Article 12 (his views given due weight) and Article 3 (best interests), and his own words go in the record. Article 31 supports the playroom he goes to afterwards.

teach.text: UNCRC vs HRA: a family in England cannot sue an NHS trust directly for breaching the UNCRC, but can bring a claim under the Human Rights Act. And Article 12 is the right to be heard, not a right to decide: the child's views are given due weight, not automatic effect.

items: UNCRC: ratified by the UK, not directly enforceable in English courts; key articles 2, 3, 12, 19, 24, 31.
HRA 1998: NHS bodies must act compatibly with ECHR rights; claims can be brought in UK courts.
ECHR articles: 2 life, 3 no degrading treatment, 5 liberty, 8 private and family life, 14 non-discrimination.
Article 12: the child's views are heard and given due weight by age and maturity.
Record the child's own words; offer real choices.

summary: You can now match nursing situations to UNCRC articles and HRA rights, and explain which framework is enforceable in English courts. You can also put Article 12 into practice by hearing and recording the child's own views.

A.q: Maya, 9, needs a nasogastric tube. The nurse lets her choose which nostril and whether to hold a parent's hand, and records what Maya said. Which UNCRC article does this most directly uphold?
options: Article 31, the right to rest, leisure and play
Article 24, the right to health and health care
Article 12, the right to be heard
Article 19, protection from violence and abuse
A.why: Article 12: children have the right to express views on matters affecting them, given due weight according to age and maturity.

whyNot.1: Article 24 concerns access to health care, not participation in decisions.

A.q: A student says a family could sue an NHS trust in an English court for breaching the UNCRC. Which response is accurate?
options: Yes, as the UK has ratified the Convention
No, it is not directly enforceable in English courts
Yes, as the HRA incorporated it in 1998
No, it applies to education and social care rather than health
A.why: The UNCRC is not directly incorporated into English law. Rights can be enforced through the Human Rights Act, which covers ECHR rights.

whyNot.0: Ratification binds the State internationally but does not make it directly enforceable in English courts.
whyNot.2: The HRA incorporated the ECHR, not the UNCRC.
whyNot.3: The UNCRC covers children's health (Article 24) too.

A.q: A ward limits parents of under-5s to two hours' visiting a day to reduce noise. Which Human Rights Act right is most engaged?
options: Article 8, respect for private and family life
Article 5, the right to liberty and security of person
Article 2, the right to life
Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
A.why: Separating young children from their parents interferes with family life (Article 8). Any restriction must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

whyNot.1: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, not visiting.
whyNot.3: Article 14 needs differential treatment linked to a status; this rule applies to all parents.

B.q: On a children's ward, the parents of Marius, 6, who are Roma, are repeatedly asked to leave at night while other parents may stay. Which Human Rights Act article is most directly breached?
options: Article 3, no inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty
Article 2, the right to life
Article 14 with Article 8
B.why: Treating one family less favourably because of ethnicity in the enjoyment of family life engages Article 14 (non-discrimination) read with Article 8.

whyNot.0: Article 3 covers severe ill-treatment; the core issue here is discriminatory treatment.
whyNot.2: There is no threat to life.

B.q: Which statement best describes the effect of the Human Rights Act 1998 on an NHS trust?
options: It must act compatibly with Convention rights
It must follow every UNCRC article in law
It may apply Convention rights to adults alone
It must seek court approval for each restriction
B.why: Public authorities, including NHS bodies, must act compatibly with Convention rights, and claims can be brought in UK courts.

whyNot.1: The HRA gives effect to the ECHR, not the UNCRC.
whyNot.2: Convention rights apply to children as well as adults.
whyNot.3: Restrictions must be justified, but not each approved by a court.

B.q: Daria, 10, has just arrived in England as an asylum seeker and is not registered with a GP. Her school nurse helps her register. Which UNCRC article best supports this?
options: Article 12, the right to be heard
Article 31, the right to play
Article 24, the right to health care
Article 3, the child's best interests
B.why: Article 24: children have the right to the highest attainable standard of health and to health care services.

whyNot.3: Best interests are relevant, but access to health care is Article 24's specific subject.

C.q: Tia, 7, is having daily dressing changes for a burn. Her mother asks staff to stop asking Tia what she wants, as 'children shouldn't make medical decisions'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as Tia is too young to consent to the dressings
Agree, and ask the mother to choose the timing instead
Explain Tia's views are heard and weighed, not decisive
Explain Tia's choice decides as the dressings are routine
C.why: Article 12 gives Tia the right to express views and have them given due weight by age and maturity. Hearing her is not the same as letting her decide whether care happens.

whyNot.0: Not being able to consent does not remove her right to be heard.
whyNot.1: Removing Tia's say in timing ignores her right to be heard.
whyNot.3: Due weight does not mean her choice decides the care.

C.q: A safeguarding nurse shares information about Kayden, 5, with children's social care because of suspected neglect. His father says this breaches his family's Article 8 rights. What is accurate?
options: Article 8 is absolute, so the sharing was unlawful
Article 8 is not engaged by sharing health information
Article 8 protects the adults and so not Kayden's own health records
Article 8 can be lawfully interfered with to protect a child
C.why: Article 8 is a qualified right. Sharing that is lawful, necessary and proportionate to protect a child can justify the interference.

whyNot.1: Sharing health information does engage Article 8; the question is justification.

C.q: A care plan for Jamie, 14, who has complex needs, records 'Jamie is happy with the plan'. Jamie uses a communication device and told staff, 'I want to go to school on Fridays.' What is the best practice?
options: Record Jamie's own words in his preferred format
Keep the summary, as it is shorter and clearer for staff
Ask his parents to confirm what Jamie meant
Record that Jamie was consulted on the plan
C.why: NICE NG213 1.4.13: record the child's own words in their preferred format and do not rewrite them. This gives effect to Article 12.

whyNot.1: A paraphrase loses Jamie's actual view.
whyNot.2: His own words should be recorded first; parents' views are additional.
whyNot.3: Noting consultation does not record what he said.

reteach.title: Standard and law
reteach.question: How do the UNCRC and the HRA differ in practice?

blocks.body: Think of the UNCRC as the promise made to every child: be heard, be safe, play, get health care, be treated equally, have your best interests come first. The Human Rights Act is the enforcer in UK courts: life, freedom from degrading treatment, liberty, private and family life, non-discrimination. A children's nurse uses both: the UNCRC to shape care, the HRA to know what the trust must legally respect.

blocks.text: Being heard (Art 12) is not deciding. UNCRC: not directly enforceable in England. HRA: enforceable against NHS bodies.

explain.body: Adopted 1989 and ratified by the UK. It guides law, policy and professional practice but is not directly incorporated into English law.

test.q: Which group does the UNCRC protect?
options: Children under 16
Children under 18
Young people under 21
Children under 13
test.why: The UNCRC applies to everyone under 18, matching the Children Act 1989 definition of a child.

whyNot.0: 16 is too low; the Convention covers under-18s.
whyNot.3: 13 is the age relevant to sexual offences, not the UNCRC.

explain.body: 2 non-discrimination; 3 best interests a primary consideration; 12 right to be heard; 19 protection from abuse; 24 health; 31 play.

test.q: Which UNCRC article makes the child's best interests a primary consideration?
options: Article 2
Article 12
Article 19
Article 3
test.why: Article 3: in all actions concerning children, their best interests are a primary consideration.

whyNot.1: Article 12 is the right to be heard.
whyNot.2: Article 19 is protection from violence and abuse.

explain.body: Public authorities must act compatibly with ECHR rights: Article 2 life, 3 no inhuman or degrading treatment, 5 liberty, 8 private and family life, 14 non-discrimination.

test.q: Leaving a child with learning disabilities in soiled bedding for hours, causing distress and humiliation, most directly engages which HRA article?
options: Article 5, liberty
Article 3, degrading treatment
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
Article 2, right to life
test.why: Treatment that humiliates and causes serious distress can amount to degrading treatment under Article 3.

whyNot.2: Article 14 needs differential treatment linked to a status.

explain.body: Article 12 and Children Act s1(3)(a) put the child's wishes and feelings first in line. Ask, listen, offer real choices, record their words.

test.q: A parent always answers questions directed to her 11-year-old son. What is the best way to hear his voice?
options: Offer him time to talk with the nurse privately
Accept the parent's account as his consent
Ask the parent to write down his views later
Give him a questionnaire to complete at home with family
test.why: Giving the child an opportunity to speak for himself, privately where appropriate, respects Article 12 and may also reveal safeguarding concerns.

whyNot.1: A parent's answers are not the child's views.
whyNot.2: The parent's written version is still not his own voice.
whyNot.3: A questionnaire at home may be completed under the same influence.
